## Problem 1: exploration of NY NOAA dataset


```{r q1_loading}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
str(ny_noaa)

#check missing var % for precipitation, snow, snow depth, maximum temperature, minimum temperature. I want to write a simple form to check all missing percentage across column instead of running 7 chunks of `mean(is.na(x))`.

ny_noaa |>
  summarise(
    across(everything(), ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100)
  )
```


This dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 key variables: `id`, `date`, precipitation (tenth of mm), snowfall (mm), snow depth (mm), maximum temperature (tenth of Celsius degree), and minimum temperature (tenth of Celsius degree). Each row represents a daily weather observation at a particular station, identifeid by `id`. No `id` or `date` is missing. However, approximately 43.71% of observations are missing maximum or minimum temperature values, which might limit the data available for temperature analyses below. Precipitation data has 5.62% of missing data, snow has 14.69% of missing data, and snow depth has 22.80% of missing data.


```{r q1_clean_separate_var}
noaa_df = ny_noaa |>
janitor::clean_names() |>
separate(date, into = c("year", "month","date"), sep = "-") |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year), 
         month = as.numeric(month), 
         date =  as.numeric(date),
         tmax_c = as.numeric(tmax)/10,
         tmin_c = as.numeric(tmin)/10,
         prcp_mm = prcp /10
  )
noaa_df |> 
    count(snow, sort = TRUE)
```


Convert observations for temperature, precipitation, and snowfall to reasonable units: Tmax and Tmin from 10th Celsius to Celsius, precipitation from tenth mm to mm. Snowfall is already recorded in milimeters and does not require conversion. 

For snowfall, the most commonly observed value is 0mm. This is expected because the dataset includes observations throughout the year. 


#### Q1.2Make a two-panel plot showing the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years. 

```{r q1_tmax_in_Jan_n_July}

tmax_df = noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(
    tmax_avg_month = mean(tmax_c, na.rm = TRUE)
  )|>
      ungroup()

#Making plot
tmax_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = tmax_avg_month, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average maximum temperature in January and July",
    subtitle = "1 = January; 7 = July.",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average daily maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

#### Q1.2.2: Is there any observable / interpretable structure? Any outliers?


Based on the plot, every year, July's average maximum temperature is much higher (around 20°C higher, estimated roughly by eyes) than January's average maximum temperature. Stations show similar year-to-year fluctuations, but January's variability is greater than July's. Around year 1987/1988, one station's average maximum temperature in July is approximately 14°C, which might be a potential outlier. There's also a low temperature an around -13.5°C in year 1982 in January's plot.


#### Q1.3 Make a two-panel plot showing (i) tmax vs tmin for the full dataset (note that a scatterplot may not be the best option); 

```{r i_tmax_vs_tmin}
temp_plot = noaa_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin_c, y = tmax_c)) +
  geom_bin2d() +
  labs(
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Number of observations"
  )

temp_plot
```


### Q1.3(ii, continue) make a plot showing the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year. 


```{r ii_snowfall}

#Making plot
snow_plot = noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, color = factor(year))) +
  geom_density() +
  labs(
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Density",
    color = "Year"
  )

snow_plot

#merge templot and snowplot
library(patchwork)

temp_plot + snow_plot
```


## Problem 2
Accelerometers have become an appealing alternative to self-report techniques for studying physical activity in observational studies and clinical trials, largely because of their relative objectivity. During observation periods, the devices can measure MIMS in a short period; one-minute intervals are common. Because accelerometers can be worn comfortably and unobtrusively, they produce around-the-clock observations.

This problem uses accelerometer data collected on 250 participants in the NHANES study. The participants’ demographic data can be downloaded here, and their accelerometer data can be downloaded here. Variables *MIMS are the MIMS values for each minute of a 24-hour day starting at midnight.



```{r loading}

covar_raw_df = read_csv(
  "./nhanes_covar.csv",
  skip = 4
) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

accel_raw_df = read_csv(
  "./nhanes_accel.csv"
) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

head(covar_raw_df)

accel_raw_df |>
  select(seqn, min1:min5) |>
  head()
```

```{r tidy&merge}
#tidy up
covar_df = covar_raw_df |>
  filter(age >=21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
mutate(
  sex = case_match(
    sex,
    1 ~ "Male",
    2 ~ "Female"
  ),
  sex = as.factor(sex),
  sex = fct_relevel(sex, "Male", "Female"),

  education = case_match(
    education,
    1 ~ "Less than high school",
    2 ~ "High school equivalent",
    3 ~ "More than high school"
  ),
  education = as.factor(education),
  education = fct_relevel(
    education,
    "Less than high school",
    "High school equivalent",
    "More than high school"
  )
)

accel_df = accel_raw_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "mims",
    names_prefix = "min"
  ) |>
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute))

#merge
q2_df = covar_df |>
  left_join(accel_df, by = "seqn")
```


### Q2. 2 Produce a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category, and create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category. 


```{r}
covar_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Education", "Men(n)", "Women(n)")
  )

covar_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, color = education)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_grid(. ~ sex) +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Density",
    color = "Education"
  )

```

228 participants remained after restricting the sample to participants aged 21+ years and excluding those with missing demographic data. There were 27 men and 28 women with less than a high school education, 35 men and 23 women with a high school equivalent education, and 56 men and 59 women with more than a high school education.

Among women, the age distribution for those with more than a high school education peaks around age 25, while the other two education groups have higher densities at older ages, forming two opposite age trends. Among men, the less-than-high-school group peaks around age 70, and has the lowest proportion among age ~ 21-30.  In this sample, higher educational level seems to associate with younger age, especially among women.



```{r}
total_activity_df = q2_df |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  summarise(
    total_activity = sum(mims)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

total_activity_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Among those with less than high school degree, since age of 40, males have higher total daily activity comparing to females. Among those with high school or more than high school degree, females tend to have higher daily activity comparing to males. Comparing across these three categories, people with less than high school degree seem to have highest total daily activity around age 21-40. All educational groups' people, regardless of their gender, total daily activity tends to be lower at older ages. 


### Q2.3 three-panel plot that shows the 24-hour activity time courses for each education level and use color to indicate sex


```{r}
daily_activity_df = q2_df |>
  group_by(sex, education, minute) |>
  summarise(
    mean_mims = mean(mims)
  ) |>
  ungroup()|>
  mutate (hour = (minute-1) /60)
  
daily_activity_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    x = "Time of the day in hours",
    y = "Mean MIMS activity per minute",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
Comparing across groups, no significant time-daily activity has been found. Three groups all seem to have lowest MIMS activity around 0-7am, then peak 7-10am, stays flat or decreases until 8pm, then decreases 8pm to 12am. However, for both sex, it seems like people with less than high school educational attainment tends to have slightly higher MIMS activity per minute, comparing to the other two groups. 


Problem 3
Citi Bike is a bike sharing system in New York City; riders can rent pedal-powered or electric bikes from starting stations and return them to another station at their destination. Introduced in 2013, the system is immensely popular and expanded rapidly. Riders who use this system often may become “members” with lower rental rates.

This zip file contains data on rides taken on the NYC Citi Bike system. Files contain 1% of all rides with a total duration less than 4 hours in each of four months. Import, clean, and tidy these data, and describe the resulting dataset.

Produce a reader-friendly table showing the total number of rides in each combination of year and month separating casual riders and Citi Bike members. Comment on these results.

Make a table showing the 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024; include the number of rides originating from these stations.

Make a plot to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration. This plot can include one or more panels, but should facilitate comparison across all variables of interest. Comment on your observations from this plot.

There were relatively few electric Citi Bikes in 2020, but many more are available now. For data in 2024, make a figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration. Comment on your results.
